title: Protocol for synthesizing and purifying short-length poly(ADP)ribose polymer
author: Neeharika, Hanuman, et al.

steps.title: Purify PARP1 via IMAC
steps.instruction: Resuspend cell pellet in lysis buffer, sonicate on ice (5 s ON, 20 s OFF, 50‑60 % amplitude, six cycles of 2.5 min; Qsonica Q125, 125 W, 25 kHz, 6.4 mm tip), centrifuge at 20 000 g for 30 min at 4 °C, and clarify the lysate. Connect a 5 mL HisTrap column to the FPLC and set flow rate to 3 mL/min. Recharge the column: 2 CV water, 3 CV stripping buffer, equilibrate with 4 CV IMAC Buffer A, rinse 2 CV water, charge with 2 CV 0.2 M NiSO₄, wash 3 CV water, re‑equilibrate 2 CV IMAC Buffer A. Load clarified supernatant (6 CV IMAC Buffer A), wash with 10 CV IMAC Buffer B, then elute with a manual gradient of IMAC Buffer C (6 %, 12 %, 24 %, 48 %, 100 %) collecting fractions. Analyze fractions by 12 % SDS‑PAGE, pool pure fractions, concentrate to 1 mL using a 30 kDa Amicon filter, perform three rounds of buffer exchange with equal volume of PARP1 Buffer D using the same filter, and finally concentrate to 10 mg/mL (≈86.2 µM) measured at 280 nm. Keep all steps at 4 °C or on ice.

substeps.instruction: Resuspend pellet in lysis buffer.
Sonicate on ice with specified settings.
Centrifuge clarified lysate at 20 000 g, 30 min, 4 °C.
Prepare HisTrap column (5 mL) at 3 mL/min flow.
Recharge column: water → stripping buffer → IMAC Buffer A → water → 0.2 M NiSO₄ → water → IMAC Buffer A.
Load supernatant, wash with Buffer B, elute with gradient of Buffer C (6‑100 %).
Analyze fractions on 12 % SDS‑PAGE, pool target fractions.
Concentrate pooled fractions to 1 mL with 30 kDa Amicon filter.
Perform three buffer‑exchange steps with PARP1 Buffer D using the same filter.
Concentrate to 10 mg/mL (86.2 µM) and measure absorbance at 280 nm.

steps.title: Prepare PAR sample for ion exchange
steps.instruction: Add 2.5 mL Buffer F to the aqueous layer containing crude PAR, connect a Resource Q column to the FPLC, set the UV detector to 254 nm, and pass 3 mL autoclaved water at 0.2 mL/min (this flow rate will be used for subsequent steps).

substeps.instruction: Add 2.5 mL Buffer F to the PAR aqueous layer.
Connect Resource Q column to FPLC.
Set detector wavelength to 254 nm.
Pass 3 mL autoclaved water at 0.2 mL/min.

steps.title: Fractionate PAR by anion exchange
steps.instruction: Equilibrate the Resource Q column with 5 mL Buffer F, load the PAR sample, wash with 10 mL Buffer F, then run a linear gradient from 0 % to 100 % Buffer G (Buffer F: 10 mM NaCl, 50 mM Tris‑HCl pH 8.0; Buffer G: 1 M NaCl, 50 mM Tris‑HCl pH 8.0) over a total volume of 200 mL at 0.25 mL/min. Collect each eluted peak manually into separate 1.5 mL vials, keep the collected fractions in a vacuum evaporator for two 2‑h cycles (total 4 h) to reduce volume, then prepare 12 µL aliquots of each evaporated sample (1–3 µL for highly concentrated peaks, 4–9 µL for medium/small peaks). Prepare control nucleic acids: 10‑mer ssDNA (100 pmol) and 16‑mer duplex DNA (100 pmol).

substeps.instruction: Equilibrate column with 5 mL Buffer F.
Load PAR sample onto column.
Wash column with 10 mL Buffer F.
Run linear gradient Buffer F (100 % → 0 %) / Buffer G (0 % → 100 %) over 200 mL at 0.25 mL/min.
Collect each peak into separate 1.5 mL vials.
Vacuum‑evaporate fractions for 4 h (two 2‑h cycles).
Prepare 12 µL of each evaporated fraction (1–3 µL for high, 4–9 µL for medium/small peaks).
Prepare 100 pmol 10‑mer ssDNA and 100 pmol 16‑mer duplex DNA controls.

steps.title: Analyze fractions by native PAGE
steps.instruction: Mix each PAR fraction and each DNA control with 1× DNA loading dye (prepared from a 6× stock) to a final volume of 12 µL, adjusting with Buffer F as needed. Load samples onto a 20 % native polyacrylamide gel and run at 80 V for 90 min or until the dye front reaches three‑quarters of the gel. Stain the gel using a standard silver‑staining protocol.

substeps.instruction: Add 1× loading dye to each sample in 12 µL total volume (adjust with Buffer F).
Load samples onto 20 % native PAGE.
Run gel at 80 V for 90 min (or until ¾ of gel).
Perform silver staining according to standard protocol.

steps.title: Concentrate and quantify PAR fractions
steps.instruction: Take the desired PAR peak fraction and concentrate it to ~0.3 mL using a Vivaspin 2‑kDa centrifugal filter (0.5–6 mL capacity) at 7000 g for 10 min; repeat the concentration step 5–6 times if needed. Add 0.3 mL autoclaved water to the filter and centrifuge back to 0.3 mL; repeat this water‑wash two more times. Finally concentrate the sample to 30–150 µL. Dilute the concentrate 1000–2000‑fold with buffer, measure absorbance at 258 nm on an Implen Nanophotometer, and calculate concentration using the ADP‑ribose extinction coefficient of 13 500 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹.

substeps.instruction: Concentrate fraction to ~0.3 mL with Vivaspin 2‑kDa filter at 7000 g, 10 min (repeat 5–6 cycles if volume is high).
Add 0.3 mL autoclaved water, centrifuge to 0.3 mL; repeat twice.
Further concentrate to 30–150 µL.
Dilute 1000–2000× and measure OD at 258 nm.
Calculate concentration using extinction coefficient 13 500 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹.

steps.title: Quantify PAR concentration
steps.instruction: Prepare dilutions of each concentrated PAR fraction and measure absorbance at 258 nm with the Nanophotometer, using the ADP‑ribose extinction coefficient (13 500 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹) to determine final polymer concentrations.

description: Poly(ADP)ribose (PAR),1,2 synthesized by PARP family enzymes, on themselves (self-PARylation) and on hundreds of other proteins, DNA, RNA, etc., using NAD+ as a substrate,3,4 regulates critical cellular processes including DNA damage repair, gene expression, chromatin remodeling, and cell death.4,5,6,7,8 Among the 17 PARP enzymes,4,9 PARP1 is the most abundant and well-studied, rapidly producing PAR chains in response to DNA damage.3,10 Its activity results in PAR chains ranging from 2 to over 244 units,11 which can be linear or branched.12 Chain length plays a key role in the function and binding specificity of PAR.12,13 Specific proteins preferentially bind short PAR chains, while others favor longer ones, impacting diverse signaling pathways.12,13,14 However, a significant barrier to structural and biophysical analysis of PAR, protein interactions is the lack of scalable, efficient, and safe protocols for generating high-purity PAR polymers of defined lengths.15,16 Most of the studies for PAR synthesis typically relied on radiolabeled NAD+, histones, HPLC purification, and enzymatic digestion (e.g., with PARG or SVP), making them expensive, hazardous, and inefficient for large-scale use.17,18 Chemical synthesis approaches remain limited to mono or di-ADPr and require specialized expertise and equipment.19
